questions.question: On a 1,024-GPU cluster, two separate synchronous training jobs each request 512 GPUs. A naive scheduler allocates 256 GPUs to each job while both wait for their remaining 256 GPUs. An hour later, both jobs have produced zero completed training steps and roughly $1,024 in GPU-hours has been burned at $2 per GPU-hour. Which systems mechanism best explains why partial allocation produced zero useful work rather than half-speed progress?
choices: Hold-and-wait deadlock: each job holds resources while waiting for more, and synchronous AllReduce requires all workers in the gang to participate in every synchronization step.
Amdahl's law bottleneck: serial portions of the training script dominate execution time, reducing parallel efficiency to zero at 256 GPUs.
Thermal throttling cascade: partially occupied nodes generate unbalanced heat profiles that trigger emergency GPU frequency throttling.
Spine-switch packet congestion: the 256 GPUs allocated per job cross multiple leaf switches, saturating bisection bandwidth.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Hold-and-wait deadlock: each job holds resources while waiting for more, and synchronous AllReduce requires all workers in the gang to participate in every synchronization step. Synchronous distributed training requires every rank to arrive at each AllReduce barrier before any worker can proceed with the next step. When each job receives only half of its required allocation, neither can complete the collective communication step, leaving all 512 allocated GPUs stalled at 0% useful throughput. Amdahl's law describes speedup limits of running code, not zero progress from missing ranks. Thermal throttling degrades clock speed rather than causing a complete collective deadlock, and network congestion increases transfer latency but does not halt execution indefinitely.
questions.learning_objective: Identify gang-scheduling deadlock as the mechanism that converts partial allocation into zero throughput for synchronous distributed training

questions.question: An operator reports that their ML training cluster experiences severe queueing delays and long wait times at 80 percent utilization, whereas their web-serving cluster operates smoothly at the same 80 percent utilization. Using the Pollaczek-Khinchine queueing model, explain why this occurs and what target utilization the operator should maintain for the ML cluster.
questions.answer: The Pollaczek-Khinchine formula establishes that normalized queue waiting time scales with utilization and the squared coefficient of variation: $W_q / (1/\mu) = \frac{\rho}{1-\rho} \cdot \frac{1+C_s^2}{2}$. For web serving with exponentially distributed service times ($C_s \approx 1$), waiting time at 80% utilization ($\rho = 0.8$) is $4\times$ the mean job duration. For ML workloads with heavy-tailed job durations (short debugging tasks mixed with multi-week pretraining runs, $C_s \approx 3$), waiting time at 80% utilization expands to $20\times$ the mean job duration—a 5-fold increase in queue delay at identical utilization. To maintain acceptable responsiveness for interactive users and short jobs, ML cluster operators must target lower sustained utilization, typically 60 to 70 percent.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how heavy-tailed ML job duration variance changes the utilization-vs-queueing trade-off and sets a lower sustainable utilization target

questions.question: On a 10,000-GPU cluster operating at $2/GPU-hour, an infrastructure optimization raises sustained productive utilization from 50 percent to 80 percent. If newly purchased GPUs would also operate at the baseline 50 percent utilization, what is the effective raw GPU equivalent gained, and what is the annual financial value of this recovered capacity?
choices: 3,000 productive GPU-equivalents gained, equivalent to procuring 6,000 raw GPUs at 50% utilization, saving $52.56M annually in productive capacity value.
3,000 productive GPU-equivalents gained, equivalent to procuring 3,000 raw GPUs at 50% utilization, saving $26.28M annually in productive capacity value.
1,500 productive GPU-equivalents gained, equivalent to procuring 3,000 raw GPUs at 50% utilization, saving $13.14M annually in productive capacity value.
6,000 productive GPU-equivalents gained, equivalent to procuring 10,000 raw GPUs at 50% utilization, saving $105.12M annually in productive capacity value.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. 3,000 productive GPU-equivalents gained, equivalent to procuring 6,000 raw GPUs at 50% utilization, saving $52.56M annually in productive capacity value. The gain in fully utilized productive capacity is $10,000 \times (0.80 - 0.50) = 3,000$ productive GPU-equivalents. If new physical accelerators operate at the old 50% utilization, delivering 3,000 productive GPU-equivalents would require purchasing $3,000 / 0.50 = 6,000$ raw GPUs. In financial terms, 3,000 productive GPUs operating 24 hours/day for 365 days at $2/GPU-hour deliver $3,000 \times 24 \times 365 \times \$2 = \$52.56\text{M}$ in annual productive value. Option B fails to account for the 50% baseline utilization of newly added hardware. Option C halves the productive capacity delta, and Option D doubles the calculated gain.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the effective capacity and financial value gained from fleet-wide utilization improvements

questions.question: In a 64-node cluster with 8 GPUs per node (512 GPUs total), a popular job template causes most jobs to request exactly 6 GPUs each. After many such jobs are scheduled, queue wait times rise sharply for pending 4-GPU and 8-GPU requests, despite the dashboard showing 25 percent of the cluster GPUs free. What systems mechanism causes this bottleneck?
choices: Spine-switch oversubscription throttles cross-node communication, preventing the scheduler from discovering free GPU resources.
Priority inversion blocks the 4-GPU and 8-GPU jobs because the 6-GPU jobs have accumulated higher fair-share decay credits.
Internal node fragmentation strands 2 GPUs on each occupied node; because NVLink-local jobs cannot combine GPUs across nodes, aggregate free capacity is decoupled from schedulable capacity.
Device driver locks prevent the NVIDIA kernel module from exposing more than 6 active contexts per physical node simultaneously.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Internal node fragmentation strands 2 GPUs on each occupied node; because NVLink-local jobs cannot combine GPUs across nodes, aggregate free capacity is decoupled from schedulable capacity. When a 6-GPU job occupies an 8-GPU node, the remaining 2 GPUs cannot be joined with residues on other nodes for workloads requiring intra-node NVLink connectivity (such as tensor parallelism or single-node jobs). While 25% of cluster GPUs sit idle globally, no single node has 4 or 8 contiguous free slots, blocking incoming requests. Network oversubscription affects data transfer performance rather than placement eligibility, fair-share decay affects queue ranking rather than physical placement feasibility, and GPU device drivers support arbitrary per-node process counts subject to memory limits.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how node-local GPU requests create cross-node fragmentation that decouples aggregate free capacity from schedulable capacity

questions.question: When an ML cluster orchestrator evaluates an incoming distributed training request requiring multi-dimensional resources (GPUs, NVLink locality, and network bandwidth), in what sequence should it apply feasibility, performance, and policy filters?
choices: 1. Rank jobs by fair-share priority $\rightarrow$ 2. Allocate partial GPUs incrementally $\rightarrow$ 3. Migrate running pods to satisfy topology constraints.

1. Verify atomic gang feasibility $\rightarrow$ 2. Filter placements by physical topology and interconnect constraints $\rightarrow$ 3. Rank feasible placements by organizational fairness and priority policy.
1. Evaluate topology locality cost $\rightarrow$ 2. Enforce department quotas $\rightarrow$ 3. Launch workers independently across available nodes.
1. Check user quota limits $\rightarrow$ 2. Interleave processes via time-slicing $\rightarrow$ 3. Validate NVLink domain matching.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. 1. Verify atomic gang feasibility -> 2. Filter placements by physical topology and interconnect constraints -> 3. Rank feasible placements by organizational fairness and priority policy. Atomic gang feasibility must be verified first because allocating partial resources to synchronous training leads directly to hold-and-wait deadlocks. Among atomically feasible allocations, the scheduler filters for physical topology constraints (e.g., placing tensor-parallel ranks within NVLink domains) because violating topology causes severe performance degradation. Finally, fairness, quotas, and priority policies rank the valid candidate placements. Allocating incrementally (Choice A) causes deadlocks, launching independently without gang checks (Choice C) strands capacity, and time-slicing before topology validation (Choice D) overlooks physical interconnect constraints.
questions.learning_objective: Order the sequence of feasibility, performance, and policy filters an ML scheduler must apply to a distributed training request

questions.question: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and preference-training pipelines co-locate policy trainers, reward model evaluators, and rollout generation workers within a single logical job. Explain why classical homogeneous gang scheduling fails for this workload and describe what scheduling capability is required instead.
questions.answer: Classical homogeneous gang scheduling assumes identical workers executing the same compute graph with identical resource profiles (e.g., $N$ identical GPUs performing synchronous data-parallel forward and backward passes). Preference-training pipelines break this homogeneity because different roles have fundamentally different computational and memory bottlenecks: rollout workers are memory- and KV-cache-bound and require high-HBM nodes for fast autoregressive generation, while policy trainers are compute-bound and require high-FLOP nodes and NVLink for backpropagation. The orchestrator must provide heterogeneous gang scheduling: atomically co-scheduling a balanced constellation of distinct hardware types and provisioning sufficient inter-role streaming bandwidth so that an under-provisioned generation tier does not starve the policy training tier.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why heterogeneous gang scheduling is required for composite ML workloads whose roles have different resource profiles

questions.question: A research team submits a batch job via 'sbatch --gres=gpu:8 --nodes=4' to a Slurm cluster, while another team submits a 4-replica PyTorchJob to a Kubernetes cluster with a controller managing pod lifecycles. Which core architectural distinction does this comparison illustrate?
choices: Slurm is restricted to Ethernet-based CPU clusters, whereas Kubernetes natively manages InfiniBand and NVLink hardware fabrics.
Slurm allocates resources exclusively at the individual process level, whereas Kubernetes schedules resources exclusively at whole-node granularity.
Slurm requires all workloads to run as containerized microservices, whereas Kubernetes executes bare-metal shell scripts without container encapsulation.

Slurm uses an imperative scheduling model that grants a one-shot atomic allocation, whereas Kubernetes uses a declarative model where control loops continuously reconcile desired state against actual state.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Slurm uses an imperative scheduling model that grants a one-shot atomic allocation, whereas Kubernetes uses a declarative model where control loops continuously reconcile desired state against actual state. Slurm's imperative model requires users to declare exact hardware resources upfront, which the centralized controller (slurmctld) allocates authoritatively for the duration of the batch job. Kubernetes uses level-triggered reconciliation loops that observe the current cluster state (stored in etcd) and continuously take corrective actions (e.g., recreating failed pods) to converge toward the declared desired state. Slurm supports high-performance InfiniBand and NVLink clusters, both schedulers can manage pod-level or node-level resources, and Kubernetes is fundamentally container-centric while Slurm typically executes jobs directly or via container wrappers.
questions.learning_objective: Differentiate imperative and declarative orchestration by the control-plane mechanism each system uses to express and enforce ML workload state

questions.question: During a 90-second network partition between the cluster control plane and a subset of worker nodes, how do Slurm and Kubernetes differ in their handling of cluster state based on the CAP theorem trade-off?
choices: Kubernetes halts all scheduling operations across the entire cluster until an administrator intervenes, whereas Slurm reassigns partitioned GPUs immediately to maximize availability.

Slurm behaves as a CP system by blocking new allocations to partitioned nodes to prevent conflicting double-allocations, whereas Kubernetes behaves as an AP system by remaining responsive and resolving state divergence asynchronously via reconciliation loops once the partition heals.
Both Slurm and Kubernetes rely on distributed Paxos consensus among worker nodes to elect a local scheduler, bypassing the central control plane entirely.
Slurm permits worker nodes to self-schedule new jobs during a partition, whereas Kubernetes terminates all workloads on disconnected nodes within 5 seconds.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Slurm behaves as a CP system by blocking new allocations to partitioned nodes to prevent conflicting double-allocations, whereas Kubernetes behaves as an AP system by remaining responsive and resolving state divergence asynchronously via reconciliation loops once the partition heals. Slurm prioritizes consistency to prevent two jobs from concurrently claiming the same expensive accelerators ($2+/GPU-hour), opting to stall scheduling decisions until authoritative node state is confirmed. Kubernetes prioritizes availability, accepting declarative updates and allowing controllers to independently converge toward the desired state once connectivity is restored. Kubernetes does not halt entirely during node partitions, neither system delegates global scheduling to worker-level Paxos consensus, and Slurm node daemons (slurmd) do not make autonomous scheduling decisions.
questions.learning_objective: Compare how Slurm and Kubernetes trade off consistency and availability during partial control-plane failures

questions.question: A 32-worker distributed training job is submitted to a vanilla Kubernetes cluster without batch scheduling extensions. Over two hours, the default scheduler places 24 pods across available nodes as capacity frees up, but the remaining 8 pods stay pending. The running pods produce zero training iterations while holding 24 GPUs. Which failure mode has occurred, and which abstraction resolves it?
choices: Partial gang allocation deadlock; resolved by introducing a PodGroup (e.g., via Volcano or Kueue) that enforces all-or-nothing scheduling before binding any pods.
Priority inversion; resolved by raising the PriorityClass of the pending pods above production serving workloads.
Container image pull back-off; resolved by pre-caching large PyTorch base images onto every worker node.
NUMA socket contention; resolved by enabling CPU core pinning and memory affinity flags in the kubelet.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Partial gang allocation deadlock; resolved by introducing a PodGroup (e.g., via Volcano or Kueue) that enforces all-or-nothing scheduling before binding any pods. The default Kubernetes scheduler evaluates and binds pods independently one at a time. For synchronous distributed training, workers cannot begin AllReduce gradient synchronization until all ranks join the communication group, so the 24 running pods sit completely idle while stranding GPUs. A PodGroup abstraction mandates that either all 32 pods (or a configured minimum threshold) are schedulable simultaneously or none are launched, eliminating partial allocation. Priority adjustments do not fix independent pod binding semantics, image caching accelerates startup but does not prevent partial allocation, and NUMA pinning optimizes memory bandwidth rather than multi-pod admission atomicity.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose Kubernetes' default partial-allocation failure mode for distributed training and identify the gang-scheduling abstraction that fixes it

questions.question: On a shared cluster of A100 GPUs, an inference team enables Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) and reports high utilization with zero noisy-neighbor interference. However, a training team on the same cluster reports that their large model training jobs face severe queue delays. Explain, in terms of partition rigidity and hardware boundaries, why both observations are accurate on the same physical hardware.
questions.answer: MIG provides hardware-level isolation by partitioning physical GPUs into fixed compute and memory slices (e.g., 1g.10gb, 3g.40gb) with dedicated memory controllers, L2 cache slices, and SMs. This completely eliminates noisy-neighbor interference for small inference services. However, MIG partition profiles are rigid: reconfiguring or merging slices requires draining all running workloads from the physical GPU first. When large training jobs arrive requiring full 8-GPU nodes connected via NVLink (or whole 7g.80gb instances), they cannot utilize the scattered, pre-configured MIG slices, even if the aggregate unallocated compute across the cluster is large. Thus, the inference team achieves isolated high density, while the training team suffers from severe capacity stranding due to partition rigidity.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the MIG utilization-versus-flexibility trade-off in mixed training-and-inference fleets

questions.question: An enterprise runs its core services on Kubernetes (leveraging its CI/CD, RBAC, and observability ecosystem) but operates large multi-month foundation model pretraining runs that require strict topology-aware gang scheduling and bare-metal MPI performance. Which architectural pattern best satisfies both requirements?
choices: A pure vanilla Kubernetes deployment with no batch extensions, relying on default pod scheduling across all training and serving nodes.
A pure Slurm deployment that replaces all web microservices and CI/CD pipelines with Slurm batch scripts.
A single cluster where every physical GPU is statically partitioned into 1g.10gb MIG slices and shared uniformly across training and inference.

A hybrid Kubernetes-over-Slurm architecture where Kubernetes manages outer workflow lifecycles and inference endpoints, while large training runs are delegated via custom operators to a dedicated Slurm partition.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. A hybrid Kubernetes-over-Slurm architecture where Kubernetes manages outer workflow lifecycles and inference endpoints, while large training runs are delegated via custom operators to a dedicated Slurm partition. This hybrid design leverages the complementary strengths of both systems: Kubernetes provides standard container lifecycle management, RBAC, service routing, and unified monitoring for the broader engineering organization, while Slurm handles the specialized, performance-critical batch training jobs where mature gang scheduling, topology awareness, and minimal runtime overhead are paramount. Pure vanilla Kubernetes (Choice A) lacks atomic gang scheduling and causes partial-allocation deadlocks. Replacing microservices with Slurm (Choice B) discards essential cloud-native serving and autoscaling infrastructure. Static MIG slicing (Choice C) destroys NVLink interconnect bandwidth and prevents large distributed training runs.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate when a hybrid Kubernetes-plus-Slurm architecture is preferable to a single-platform design

questions.question: An 8-way tensor-parallel model group runs at near-ideal iteration time when placed on a single 8-GPU node via NVLink, but exhibits a 15 to 30 percent end-to-end training slowdown when split across two nodes connected by NDR InfiniBand (4 GPUs per node). What physical systems mechanism causes this performance drop?
choices: InfiniBand switches drop all packets containing tensor-parallel activations due to MTU size limits, triggering software-emulated TCP fallbacks.
Cross-node placement disables GPU CUDA streams, forcing all forward and backward matrix multiplications to execute sequentially on the host CPU.

Tensor parallelism exchanges activation and gradient slices at every transformer layer; NVLink provides 450 GB/s per direction with sub-microsecond latency, whereas NDR InfiniBand provides ~50 GB/s, forcing intermediate tensor transfers onto the exposed critical path.
Two nodes in the same rack share a single PCIe root complex, creating memory bus saturation across the host CPU sockets.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Tensor parallelism exchanges activation and gradient slices at every transformer layer; NVLink provides 450 GB/s per direction with sub-microsecond latency, whereas NDR InfiniBand provides ~50 GB/s, forcing intermediate tensor transfers onto the exposed critical path. Because large language models contain dozens of layers (e.g., 80+ layers), tensor parallel communication occurs multiple times per layer in the forward and backward passes. Intra-node NVLink provides high enough bandwidth (450 GB/s per direction on H100) to overlap or rapidly complete these transfers. Crossing to inter-node InfiniBand (50 GB/s per link) introduces an order-of-magnitude bandwidth reduction and higher latency that cannot be hidden by computation, directly inflating step time. InfiniBand fabrics do not drop tensor packets due to MTU limits, GPU CUDA streams remain operational across nodes, and distinct physical nodes have independent PCIe and NUMA complexes.
questions.learning_objective: Identify why tensor-parallel workloads are especially sensitive to intra-node NVLink locality versus inter-node InfiniBand

questions.question: A distributed training job uses 3D parallelism: 8-way tensor parallelism (TP), 4-way pipeline parallelism (PP), and 8-way data parallelism (DP), totaling 256 GPUs across 32 nodes (8 GPUs per node). Explain how a topology-aware scheduler should map these three parallelism dimensions across the cluster's network hierarchy (intra-node, intra-rack, and cross-rack).
questions.answer:
The scheduler must align the communication frequency and bandwidth intensity of each parallelism dimension with the corresponding tier of the physical network hierarchy:
1. Tensor Parallelism (8-way): Must be confined strictly within a single node (8 GPUs) to exploit intra-node NVLink (450 GB/s per direction), because TP exchanges activation and gradient tensors at every transformer layer.
2. Pipeline Parallelism (4-way): Adjacent pipeline stages should be placed on consecutive nodes within the same rack under a shared leaf switch. PP transfers activations and gradients only at stage boundaries once per micro-batch, which intra-rack InfiniBand (50 GB/s, single switch hop) can readily accommodate.
3. Data Parallelism (8-way): DP replicas can be distributed across racks crossing spine switches. DP AllReduce gradient synchronization occurs once per step and can be overlapped asynchronously with backward compute passes, making it resilient to multi-hop cross-rack bisection latency.
questions.learning_objective: Apply topology-aware placement principles to a three-dimensional parallelism configuration

questions.question: For a 1 GB gradient AllReduce synchronization across 64 GPUs, empirical measurements show latencies of 120 ms for random placement, 85 ms for rack-aware placement, 40 ms for rail-optimized placement, and 25 ms for topology-optimal placement. What is the fundamental takeaway from this 4.8x performance spread?
choices: Random placement achieves higher hardware efficiency because spreading traffic across all spine switches maximizes global link utilization.
Rail optimization is only effective for CPU memory transfers and has zero impact on GPU gradient synchronization.

Network placement alone—without modifying model architecture, batch size, or optimizer code—dramatically accelerates collective communication by minimizing switch hops, avoiding spine congestion, and leveraging dedicated network rails.
Collective communication latency is determined exclusively by the GPU floating-point engine and is independent of network switch topology.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Network placement alone—without modifying model architecture, batch size, or optimizer code—dramatically accelerates collective communication by minimizing switch hops, avoiding spine congestion, and leveraging dedicated network rails. Ring and tree AllReduce performance depends directly on the bandwidth and latency of the slowest physical link in the collective. Random placement scatters ranks across racks, forcing traffic across multiple leaf-spine-leaf switch hops subject to oversubscription and packet contention (120 ms). Confining ranks to a single leaf switch or aligning them to dedicated InfiniBand rails eliminates cross-switch contention and reduces hop count, cutting latency to 25 ms (a 4.8x communication speedup). Spreading traffic randomly increases tail latency rather than efficiency, rail optimization specifically optimizes GPU AllReduce across network rails, and collective synchronization is heavily network-bound rather than compute-bound.
questions.learning_objective: Quantify the impact of topology-aware placement on collective-communication performance

questions.question: Why is static topology configuration (such as static Slurm 'topology.conf' files or static Kubernetes node labels) insufficient for maintaining optimal placement in production GPU clusters?
choices: Static configuration files cannot represent network topologies with more than two hierarchical switch tiers.
Modern collective communication libraries like NCCL ignore physical network devices unless topology is updated dynamically via DNS records.
Static topology files disable GPU direct memory access (GPUDirect RDMA) across physical PCIe switches.

Static configurations reflect only the intended physical wiring diagram; degraded transceivers, packet retransmissions, and switch link flap cause runtime bandwidth collapse ('limping switches') that pass binary up/down health checks while crippling AllReduce throughput.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Static configurations reflect only the intended physical wiring diagram; degraded transceivers, packet retransmissions, and switch link flap cause runtime bandwidth collapse ('limping switches') that pass binary up/down health checks while crippling AllReduce throughput. In large fabrics, hardware degradation often manifests as brownouts rather than complete fail-stop link failures (e.g., bit-error rates causing link speed degradation from 100 Gbps to 1 Gbps). A static map marks the link as healthy, leading the scheduler to place large distributed training runs across the degraded path where synchronous AllReduce stalls all workers. Production schedulers require runtime introspection (e.g., NCCL link probing, DCGM counters, packet error telemetry) to quarantine degraded links dynamically. Static files can represent arbitrary multi-tier topologies, NCCL discovers topology via local system interfaces (/sys/class/infiniband) rather than DNS, and GPUDirect RDMA is controlled by kernel drivers rather than static scheduler files.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate why production scheduling must track effective runtime topology rather than static intended topology

questions.question: In a rail-optimized network fabric where each GPU in an 8-GPU node connects to an independent network switch rail, which placement strategy maximizes data-parallel AllReduce efficiency?
choices: Assign data-parallel rank $r$ to GPU index $r \bmod 8$ across all allocated nodes, ensuring that AllReduce for each group is isolated to a single rail's dedicated switch hierarchy without cross-rail contention.
Distribute data-parallel ranks randomly across available GPU indices on each node to maximize multi-path switch entropy.
Place all data-parallel workers on GPU index 0 of every node and leave GPU indices 1 through 7 unallocated.
Alternate adjacent data-parallel ranks between GPU 0 and GPU 7 to balance thermal dissipation across the server chassis.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Assign data-parallel rank r to GPU index r mod 8 across all allocated nodes, ensuring that AllReduce for each group is isolated to a single rail's dedicated switch hierarchy without cross-rail contention. Rail-optimized fabrics connect GPU 0 on every node to Rail 0, GPU 1 to Rail 1, and so forth. By aligning data-parallel groups to the same local GPU index across nodes, the entire AllReduce collective for that group traverses only that rail's dedicated switch tree. This prevents traffic from different data-parallel groups from crossing rails and contending at shared switch ports. Random assignment (Choice B) mixes traffic across rails, causing severe switch buffer contention and head-of-line blocking. Stranding GPU slots (Choice C) wastes 87.5% of cluster capacity, and alternating for thermal reasons (Choice D) violates rail alignment without meaningful thermal benefit.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the rail-alignment rule that exploits rail-optimized topologies for data-parallel AllReduce

questions.question: A spine switch failure halves cross-rack bisection bandwidth for an active foundation model training run that has three weeks of compute remaining, causing a 20 percent step-time regression. Checkpointing, rescheduling on healthy nodes, and warming up takes 15 minutes. Explain how the scheduler determines whether to migrate the job or let it continue on the degraded network.
questions.answer:
The scheduler evaluates the break-even trade-off between the one-time migration cost and the cumulative lost compute time on the degraded network:
1. Migration cost: A fixed overhead of 15 minutes ($0.25$ hours) for checkpoint save, process teardown, rescheduling, weight reload, and warmup.
2. Degraded throughput cost: A 20% step-time penalty over three weeks ($3 \times 7 \times 24 = 504$ hours) wastes $504 \times 0.20 = 100.8$ hours of productive GPU time.
Because 100.8 hours of lost throughput vastly exceeds the 0.25-hour migration overhead, the scheduler should immediately trigger migration. In general, the break-even point occurs when $\text{Time}_{\text{remaining}} \times \text{Slowdown} \ge \text{Cost}_{\text{migration}}$. Here, break-even is reached in just $15 / 0.20 = 75$ minutes of training, making migration overwhelmingly beneficial for long-running jobs.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate topology-aware migration decisions as a quantitative trade-off between migration overhead and degraded-bandwidth throughput loss

questions.question: What is the primary cluster-level scheduling advantage of submitting a distributed training job with an elastic worker range (e.g., 32 to 128 GPUs) rather than a fixed request for 128 GPUs?
choices: Elastic jobs automatically bypass all gradient synchronization barriers and run fully asynchronously without loss of convergence accuracy.
The job can be admitted immediately on a minimum viable allocation (32 GPUs) to make continuous training progress while waiting for additional capacity, dramatically reducing queue wait time.
The job achieves perfectly linear speedup across all intermediate worker counts, eliminating scaling efficiency roll-off.
Elastic training removes the requirement for persistent checkpoint storage because worker failures never cause lost steps.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The job can be admitted immediately on a minimum viable allocation (32 GPUs) to make continuous training progress while waiting for additional capacity, dramatically reducing queue wait time. In congested clusters, large gang-scheduled jobs often wait hours or days for a full contiguous block of 128 GPUs. With an elastic range $[N_{\text{min}}, N_{\text{max}}]$, the scheduler admits the job as soon as $N_{\text{min}}$ (32 GPUs) are free, productively advancing training and dynamically absorbing newly freed nodes up to $N_{\text{max}}$. Elasticity does not make training asynchronous (workers still synchronize gradients via collectives), scaling efficiency remains subject to communication overhead and diminishing returns, and elastic jobs still require checkpoints and rendezvous mechanisms to handle worker additions and removals safely.
questions.learning_objective: Identify how elastic resource ranges reduce queueing delay for distributed training without removing the underlying coordination requirements

questions.question: Describe the bidirectional contract required between a cluster scheduler and a distributed training framework (such as TorchElastic) to enable safe elastic scaling without corrupting model state.
questions.answer:
Safe elastic scaling requires explicit guarantees from both sides:
1. Scheduler responsibilities: The scheduler must communicate resource adjustments through defined signals (e.g., SIGTERM with preemption grace periods or coordination RPCs), provide sufficient advance notice (typically 10 to 60 seconds) for graceful checkpointing/rendezvous, and enforce scaling policies that respect the job's minimum viable scale $[N_{\text{min}}, N_{\text{max}}]$ without causing thrashing.
2. Framework responsibilities: The framework must handle membership changes gracefully by reconstructing collective communication groups (re-rendezvous), redistributing dataset shards across the new worker count, and adjusting training hyperparameters (e.g., maintaining global batch size via gradient accumulation or adaptively recalibrating the learning rate) so model convergence is not compromised.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the coordination contract between orchestration and training frameworks in elastic training

questions.question: Why is dynamic elastic scaling straightforward to apply to data-parallel distributed training but exceptionally difficult to apply to tensor-parallel training?
choices: Tensor parallelism does not use GPU memory, making memory allocation tracking impossible for the cluster scheduler.
Data parallelism does not require network communication between workers, whereas tensor parallelism requires continuous CPU disk writes.
Elastic frameworks like TorchElastic are mathematically restricted to single-node deployments and cannot run across multiple servers.

Data parallelism scales by adding or removing whole model replicas while keeping the per-model computation graph identical, whereas tensor parallelism shards individual weight matrices across GPUs, requiring complete tensor re-sharding and communication rebuilding if group size changes.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Data parallelism scales by adding or removing whole model replicas while keeping the per-model computation graph identical, whereas tensor parallelism shards individual weight matrices across GPUs, requiring complete tensor re-sharding and communication rebuilding if group size changes. In data-parallel training, changing worker count simply alters the number of independent model copies and the size of the gradient AllReduce ring. In tensor parallelism (e.g., Megatron-LM), weight tensors within every multi-head attention and MLP block are partitioned across a fixed intra-node group (typically 8 GPUs over NVLink). Removing or adding a GPU within a tensor-parallel group requires re-partitioning every model parameter, adjusting matrix multiplication dimensions, and reloading weights—equivalent to a full restart. Tensor parallelism heavily utilizes GPU HBM, data parallelism requires gradient AllReduce communication across workers, and TorchElastic natively orchestrates multi-node clusters.
questions.learning_objective: Compare the elasticity constraints of data-parallel versus tensor-parallel training

questions.question: When an elastic data-parallel job scales down from 256 GPUs to 64 GPUs, which fundamental trade-off must the training framework navigate regarding batch size and GPU memory limits?
choices: Scaling down automatically increases GPU clock frequencies to compensate for the missing workers, maintaining identical throughput without memory changes.

Holding global batch size constant preserves optimization convergence but requires $4\times$ larger per-GPU activation memory (or gradient accumulation), risking out-of-memory errors; holding per-GPU batch size constant avoids OOMs but shrinks global batch size, requiring adaptive learning-rate recalibration to avoid convergence drift.
Holding per-GPU batch size constant violates IEEE 754 floating-point precision standards during backpropagation.
Holding global batch size constant eliminates the need for optimizer state tracking in GPU memory.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Holding global batch size constant preserves optimization convergence but requires 4x larger per-GPU activation memory (or gradient accumulation), risking out-of-memory errors; holding per-GPU batch size constant avoids OOMs but shrinks global batch size, requiring adaptive learning-rate recalibration to avoid convergence drift. The effective global batch size is $B_{\text{global}} = N \times B_{\text{per-worker}}$. If the framework maintains $B_{\text{global}}$ constant across 64 GPUs instead of 256, each remaining worker must process $4\times$ as many samples per step, increasing activation memory pressure and risking OOM unless micro-batching with gradient accumulation is used. Conversely, keeping $B_{\text{per-worker}}$ constant reduces $B_{\text{global}}$ by $4\times$, which alters stochastic gradient noise and necessitates adjusting learning rate schedules (e.g., linear or square-root scaling rules) to preserve convergence trajectory. GPU clocks do not dynamically quadruple, IEEE 754 precision is unaffected by batch sizing, and optimizer states remain mandatory for gradient updates.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the trade-off between constant global batch size and adaptive learning rate when scaling an elastic job down

questions.question: An orchestrator must decide whether to scale an elastic training job from 128 GPUs to 256 GPUs. In what sequence should the scheduler evaluate this scaling decision?
choices: 1. Preempt 128 lower-priority GPUs immediately $\rightarrow$ 2. Check if the job supports elasticity $\rightarrow$ 3. Measure resulting throughput post-facto.
1. Trigger framework rendezvous $\rightarrow$ 2. Double global learning rate $\rightarrow$ 3. Allocate physical node leases.

1. Profile or look up the job's empirical scaling efficiency curve $\rightarrow$ 2. Verify that marginal throughput gains exceed checkpoint and group reconfiguration overhead $\rightarrow$ 3. Signal framework to execute rendezvous and resize.
1. Verify that cluster utilization is below 50% $\rightarrow$ 2. Force model re-sharding across NVLink $\rightarrow$ 3. Check for OOM errors.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. 1. Profile or look up the job's empirical scaling efficiency curve -> 2. Verify that marginal throughput gains exceed checkpoint and group reconfiguration overhead -> 3. Signal framework to execute rendezvous and resize. The scheduler must first determine where the job lies on its scaling efficiency curve ($\eta(k)$): if the job is already in the saturation phase where communication overhead dominates, adding GPUs yields negligible throughput gain. Second, the scheduler must calculate whether the marginal speedup will amortize the transition tax (10 to 60 seconds of pausing, state redistribution, and warmup) over the expected remaining runtime. Only after these cost-benefit checks pass does the scheduler allocate nodes and signal the framework to trigger re-rendezvous. Preempting before verifying elasticity (Choice A) risks unnecessary job kills, triggering rendezvous before allocation (Choice B) causes framework crashes, and blind re-sharding (Choice D) damages model state.
questions.learning_objective: Order the policy steps required to make a well-reasoned elastic-scaling decision

questions.question: A cluster policy aggressively resizes elastic jobs whenever a single node frees up or is claimed by a new arrival, resulting in resizing events every 3 to 5 minutes. Explain why this policy reduces overall training throughput rather than maximizing it, and describe the mechanism used to prevent this failure mode.
questions.answer: Every elastic scaling transition incurs a non-zero overhead tax: pausing workers, saving or transferring state, executing distributed rendezvous, rebuilding communication communicators, redistributing data batches, and warming up GPU caches (typically taking 10 to 60 seconds). If re-scaling occurs every 3 to 5 minutes, the job spends 10 to 30 percent of its total wall-clock time in coordination overhead rather than advancing training, creating a state of continuous thrashing. To prevent this, production schedulers implement scaling hysteresis: they enforce minimum marginal-utility thresholds (only scaling if the expected throughput gain exceeds a substantial percentage) and cooldown windows (e.g., forbidding re-scaling within 15 to 30 minutes of the previous resize event) so short-term capacity fluctuations do not disrupt execution.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate why elastic-scaling policies must account for transition overhead and thrashing risk

questions.question: Why does the chapter characterize cluster utilization improvement (e.g., raising fleet utilization from 50 percent to 80 percent) as one of the highest-leverage financial investments in ML infrastructure?
choices: Because improving utilization on existing hardware delivers thousands of productive GPU-equivalents of compute without incurring capital procurement costs or increasing baseline data center power and cooling capacity.
Because higher utilization automatically reduces software licensing fees paid to GPU manufacturers by a factor of two.
Because raising utilization eliminates the need for fault-tolerant checkpoint storage systems.
Because clusters operating above 95% utilization completely eliminate job queue wait times for researchers.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Because improving utilization on existing hardware delivers thousands of productive GPU-equivalents of compute without incurring capital procurement costs or increasing baseline data center power and cooling capacity. On a 10,000-GPU cluster representing hundreds of millions of dollars in capital expenditure, moving sustained productive utilization from 50% to 80% yields 3,000 additional productive GPU-equivalents—equivalent to procuring 6,000 raw GPUs running at the baseline 50% efficiency ($52.56M in annual compute value). Because the physical hardware, rack space, power infrastructure, and cooling are already paid for, this capacity is unlocked purely through software orchestration and policy tuning. Software licensing fees are a minor fraction of TCO, checkpoint storage remains mandatory regardless of utilization, and very high utilization (>90%) dramatically increases queue wait times rather than eliminating them.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate how utilization improvements substitute for hardware procurement by converting existing capacity into additional productive GPU-hours

questions.question: Spot instances offer 60 to 90 percent discounts compared to on-demand cloud pricing. Using the effective cost formula $C_{\text{effective}} = C_{\text{spot}} \times \frac{T_{\text{total}}}{T_{\text{productive}}}$, explain when spot training becomes more expensive than on-demand, and identify the fault-tolerance properties that preserve the discount.
questions.answer:
Effective spot cost is the nominal spot price scaled by the ratio of total wall-clock time ($T_{\text{total}}$) to productive training time ($T_{\text{productive}}$). $T_{\text{total}}$ includes productive training plus checkpoint overhead, restart delays, and lost compute between the last checkpoint and each preemption event. If interruptions are frequent (e.g., every 2 hours) and checkpoint/restart overhead is large (e.g., 45 minutes of state reloading and lost work for a 100B+ parameter model), $T_{\text{total}} / T_{\text{productive}}$ can exceed $3\times$ to $4\times$, completely erasing a 65% spot discount and making spot training more expensive than on-demand. To preserve the spot discount, the fault-tolerance stack must provide:
1. Fast, asynchronous checkpointing (minimizing overhead to <5% of runtime),
2. Rapid checkpoint loading and warmup (sub-minute state restoration), and
3. Termination-notice-triggered checkpointing or elastic shrink capabilities that capture state before eviction.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze when interruption overhead erases the headline discount of spot capacity and identify the fault-tolerance properties that preserve it

questions.question: Which workload archetype is the most economically appropriate candidate for long-term reserved cloud capacity (1- to 3-year commitments at 30 to 60 percent discount) rather than spot or on-demand instances?
choices: A 24/7 production LLM inference service with strict P99 latency SLOs and predictable baseline customer traffic.
A disposable hyperparameter exploration sweep where trials can be preempted without checkpointing.
An interactive one-off debugging session requiring immediate 10-minute GPU access.
A batch data tokenization pipeline that runs exclusively on weekend nights.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. A 24/7 production LLM inference service with strict P99 latency SLOs and predictable baseline customer traffic. Reserved capacity requires multi-year financial commitments in exchange for guaranteed, non-preemptible hardware availability. Production inference requires continuous 24/7 uptime and cannot tolerate preemption or capacity reclamation, making reserved instances the optimal match. Disposable sweeps (Choice B) belong on spot capacity where massive discounts outweigh preemption risk. Interactive debugging (Choice C) is best served by flexible on-demand capacity to avoid long-term commitment. Off-peak weekend batch jobs (Choice D) should utilize opportunistically borrowed capacity or spot pools.
questions.learning_objective: Classify workloads by the most economically appropriate capacity tier

questions.question: Why does the chapter state that investments in ML fault tolerance infrastructure deliver a 'double return' on investment?
choices: Fault tolerance doubles the floating-point arithmetic throughput of tensor cores while cutting DRAM power consumption in half.
Fault tolerance eliminates all software bugs in the training framework while automating hyperparameter selection.

Fault tolerance infrastructure protects against involuntary hardware failures during multi-week training runs AND unlocks voluntary cost savings by making discounted, interruptible spot instances economically viable.
Fault tolerance allows on-premise clusters to charge external cloud providers for idle capacity.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Fault tolerance infrastructure protects against involuntary hardware failures during multi-week training runs AND unlocks voluntary cost savings by making discounted, interruptible spot instances economically viable. The primary motivation for building fast checkpointing, elastic recovery, and automated health probing is reliability (preventing lost work from routine hardware failures at scale). However, this exact same technical capability reduces the cost per interruption to near zero, enabling the organization to run large training runs on 60–90% discounted spot capacity. Thus, a single infrastructure investment yields dual returns in reliability assurance and cloud cost reduction. Fault tolerance does not alter physical tensor core FLOPs, fix software bugs, or create external cloud billing capabilities.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why investments in ML fault tolerance improve both reliability and cost efficiency

questions.question: An organization is evaluating whether to build an on-premise 1,000-GPU cluster or rent GPU capacity in the cloud. Explain why average cluster utilization is the critical break-even variable in this Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculation.
questions.answer: On-premise infrastructure converts compute into a high fixed cost through capital expenditure (silicon, networking, parallel storage, power delivery, liquid cooling) and ongoing facilities operations. The effective cost per productive GPU-hour on-premise is inversely proportional to utilization: at 90% utilization, fixed costs are amortized over many productive hours, yielding low cost per hour; at 30% utilization, the cost per productive hour triples. Cloud rental, conversely, represents a variable pay-per-use cost with elastic scaling. The financial break-even point is the utilization threshold where amortized on-premise TCO per productive GPU-hour equals the cloud rate. Below this utilization threshold, cloud rental is cheaper despite higher nominal hourly rates; above it, owned hardware achieves substantial cost savings.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how utilization determines the TCO break-even point between cloud and owned infrastructure

questions.question: What fundamental limitation of general-purpose cluster schedulers (like standard Slurm or default Kubernetes) motivates the development of domain-specific ML schedulers such as Tiresias, Gandiva, and Pollux?
choices: General-purpose schedulers cannot place workloads on nodes that contain more than 16 GB of system RAM.

General-purpose schedulers treat training jobs as opaque black-box resource consumers, discarding domain-specific signals such as attained GPU-time, iteration boundaries, loss convergence curves, and batch-size scaling efficiency.
General-purpose schedulers are legally prohibited from executing Python-based machine learning frameworks.
General-purpose schedulers are restricted to single-threaded CPU architectures and cannot communicate with PCIe buses.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. General-purpose schedulers treat training jobs as opaque black-box resource consumers, discarding domain-specific signals such as attained GPU-time, iteration boundaries, loss convergence curves, and batch-size scaling efficiency. Generic schedulers view a job as static resource requests (e.g., 'give me 64 GPUs for 72 hours') and schedule via basic FIFO or fair-share queues. ML workloads, however, emit rich domain signals: iterative loops with clean context-switching boundaries, heavy-tailed duration distributions where past consumption predicts remaining duration, and elastic throughput curves that change with batch size. Custom ML schedulers exploit these internal dynamics to minimize average job completion time, enable cheap preemption, and co-tune hyperparameters. Generic schedulers support arbitrary memory capacities, execute any user containers, and manage PCIe-attached devices.
questions.learning_objective: Identify why ML-specific workload signals can improve scheduling beyond generic resource allocation

questions.question: Which custom ML scheduler addresses the problem of inaccurate user-provided runtime estimates by prioritizing jobs based on two-dimensional attained service (GPU-hours consumed) rather than predicted durations?
choices: Gandiva
Themis
Pollux
Tiresias
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Tiresias sidesteps inaccurate user runtime estimates by prioritizing jobs based on attained service (the product of allocated GPUs and elapsed runtime). In ML clusters, job durations follow a heavy-tailed distribution (many short trials, few massive runs). Because users routinely overestimate runtimes to avoid preemption, shortest-job-first policies fail. Tiresias discretizes attained service into priority bins, promoting newly arrived jobs with low attained service to the front of the queue and gradually deprioritizing long-running jobs. This approximates shortest-remaining-processing-time (SRPT) without requiring future runtime knowledge. Gandiva focuses on iteration-boundary time-slicing, Themis optimizes finish-time fairness, and Pollux co-tunes batch size and GPU allocation.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the ML scheduler designed to avoid dependence on user-supplied runtime estimates

questions.question: Explain why Gandiva uses iteration boundaries as the primary preemption and context-switching point for GPU time-slicing, and why preempting mid-iteration would be significantly worse.
questions.answer: At an iteration boundary, the forward and backward passes for a mini-batch have completed and the optimizer update has executed. At this exact point, all intermediate activation tensors (which consume gigabytes of memory per layer) have been deallocated; the GPU retains only the model weights and optimizer state. Pausing a job at an iteration boundary requires saving only this compact model state, making context switching fast (seconds). Resuming simply involves streaming the next mini-batch. Preempting mid-iteration would force the system to save the massive, dynamic activation stack from GPU memory to host RAM or disk and restore it before resuming the backward pass, incurring high I/O latency, memory fragmentation, and risk of CUDA context corruption.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why iteration boundaries are the natural preemption point for deep learning workloads

questions.question: What architectural capability gives Pollux higher cluster-wide efficiency gains than Tiresias, while also introducing a significantly higher operational risk for production ML teams?
choices: Pollux replaces all GPU drivers with custom assembly routines, risking hardware damage to tensor cores.

Pollux jointly co-tunes GPU allocation AND training hyperparameters (batch size and learning rate) based on a goodput model; if the goodput model mispredicts statistical efficiency, it can corrupt model convergence rather than merely delaying queue times.
Pollux requires all training jobs to be hosted on single-socket CPU nodes without network interconnects.
Pollux converts all floating-point calculations to 4-bit integer representations without user consent.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Pollux jointly co-tunes GPU allocation AND training hyperparameters (batch size and learning rate) based on a goodput model; if the goodput model mispredicts statistical efficiency, it can corrupt model convergence rather than merely delaying queue times. Tiresias operates strictly at the queue level by reordering jobs based on attained service—a bad scheduling decision only alters wait time. Pollux, by contrast, actively modifies the training loop's internal hyperparameters, scaling batch size and GPU count to maximize goodput (system throughput $\times$ statistical efficiency). If Pollux's empirical model misestimates gradient noise scale or if a model cannot tolerate dynamic batch resizing, training can diverge or reach sub-optimal validation accuracy. Pollux uses standard drivers, supports multi-node fabrics, and does not alter numerical precision arbitrarily.
questions.learning_objective: Compare the optimization scope and risk profile of Pollux against simpler ML-aware schedulers

questions.question: Why is minimizing average Job Completion Time (JCT)—the primary optimization target of research schedulers like Tiresias—often dangerous when applied indiscriminately as the sole objective in an enterprise production cluster?
choices: Optimizing solely for average JCT systematically favors thousands of tiny debugging and hyperparameter trials while repeatedly preempting or starving large, mission-critical foundation model training runs that drive core business value.
Minimizing average JCT causes physical wear on NVLink interconnect copper traces due to high packet frequencies.
Average JCT optimization is mathematically impossible on clusters containing more than 100 GPUs.
Minimizing average JCT requires encrypting all training datasets with public-key cryptography.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Optimizing solely for average JCT systematically favors thousands of tiny debugging and hyperparameter trials while repeatedly preempting or starving large, mission-critical foundation model training runs that drive core business value. Under an unconstrained shortest-remaining-processing-time or attained-service policy, an influx of short 10-minute experiments will continually preempt a multi-month 1,024-GPU pretraining run because clearing many short jobs dramatically lowers the mathematical average completion time across all jobs. In an enterprise, however, the multi-million-dollar pretraining run has strict delivery deadlines. Production schedulers must therefore enforce Quality of Service (QoS) tiers, dedicated partitions, or starvation-prevention guards rather than optimizing an unweighted aggregate metric. JCT optimization does not cause physical wire wear, scales to large clusters, and has no relation to dataset cryptography.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate why a single aggregate scheduling metric can conflict with production workload priorities

questions.question: An infrastructure platform team wants to adopt techniques from ML-aware research schedulers but is hesitant to modify deep learning training scripts or risk model convergence failures. Which scheduler design should they adopt as a starting point, and why?
questions.answer: The team should adopt a Tiresias-style attained-service scheduler. Tiresias operates entirely at the control plane / queue level without requiring changes to user model code, loss functions, or hyperparameter schedules. It measures only external, observable resource consumption (GPU-hours consumed per job) and reorders queue priorities using multi-level feedback queues. Because it never modifies batch sizes, learning rates, or internal execution graphs, its failure blast radius is strictly confined to queue wait-time ordering: in the worst case, a job waits slightly longer, but training correctness and convergence dynamics are 100% preserved. This provides 40 to 60 percent of the average JCT reduction benefits with zero framework-level convergence risk.
questions.learning_objective: Justify a production adoption path for ML-aware scheduling based on operational risk

questions.question: Why is raw GPU compute utilization (e.g., streaming multiprocessor busyness) a dangerous and unreliable primary metric for autoscaling LLM inference services?
choices: GPU compute utilization metrics can only be polled once every 24 hours due to kernel driver limitations.
Compute utilization on GPUs is always 100% regardless of whether any models are loaded or executing.
LLM inference runs exclusively on host CPU cores and never activates GPU compute silicon.

LLM inference is heavily memory-capacity bound by the Key-Value (KV) cache; a sudden influx of long-context requests can exhaust GPU memory and cause request dropping or latency spikes while compute utilization remains low.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. LLM inference is heavily memory-capacity bound by the Key-Value (KV) cache; a sudden influx of long-context requests can exhaust GPU memory and cause request dropping or latency spikes while compute utilization remains low. In autoregressive transformer decoding, model weights are fixed, but the KV cache grows dynamically with sequence length and concurrent active requests. When long-context requests arrive (e.g., document summarization), memory capacity can reach 100% saturation—triggering out-of-memory errors or request queueing—while arithmetic SM utilization remains modest (e.g., 30–50%). An autoscaler monitoring only compute utilization will fail to scale out, causing severe SLO violations. GPU telemetry is polled at sub-second intervals via DCGM, idle GPUs report near 0% utilization, and LLMs execute matrix math on GPU tensor cores.
questions.learning_objective: Identify why GPU memory pressure and queue depth must augment compute utilization for inference autoscaling

questions.question: A reactive autoscaler (such as Kubernetes HPA) triggers scale-up only after traffic crosses a utilization threshold, whereas a predictive autoscaler forecasts demand curves. Explain why predictive autoscaling is necessary to prevent SLO violations for large language model serving, referencing the cold-start timeline.
questions.answer: Large language model serving instances suffer from multi-minute cold-start latencies. For example, a 70B parameter model in FP16 requires loading 140 GB of weights from storage into GPU memory, initializing CUDA contexts, compiling computation graphs, and executing warmup queries—a process typically taking 60 to 180 seconds. A reactive autoscaler detects a traffic surge only after capacity is saturated, opening a 1- to 3-minute gap during which all excess incoming requests accumulate in backlogs or get dropped, severely violating latency SLOs. A predictive autoscaler uses diurnal traffic forecasts and leading indicators to trigger replica provisioning 3 to 5 minutes before the traffic surge arrives, ensuring that newly initialized replicas are warm and ready at the exact moment demand peaks.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why predictive autoscaling is necessary for large-model serving to overcome cold-start latency

questions.question: Which GPU resource-sharing mechanism provides true hardware-level fault, performance, and memory bandwidth isolation between multi-tenant inference workloads on an NVIDIA A100 or H100 GPU?
choices: CUDA Multi-Process Service (MPS), which relies on software context interleaving with shared memory address spaces.
OS-level cgroups, which enforce kernel thread CPU limits across host motherboard sockets.
Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), which partitions physical GPUs into dedicated hardware slices with private memory controllers, L2 cache slices, and SM compute engines.
CUDA Time-Slicing, which context-switches entire compute passes without memory isolation.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), which partitions physical GPUs into dedicated hardware slices with private memory controllers, L2 cache slices, and SM compute engines. MIG enforces isolation at the physical silicon level: each instance receives guaranteed fractions of GPU memory, independent memory bandwidth paths, dedicated L2 cache banks, and isolated SMs. A memory leak, crash, or intense memory-bus activity in one MIG slice has zero physical effect on neighboring slices. MPS (Choice A) multiplexes kernels from multiple processes over shared memory controllers and L2 cache, meaning an out-of-memory crash in one client crashes the entire MPS server. Host cgroups (Choice B) manage CPU/host RAM but have no hardware control over GPU memory buses. CUDA time-slicing (Choice D) round-robins compute but provides zero memory or cache isolation.
questions.learning_objective: Compare hardware-level and software-level GPU isolation mechanisms for multi-tenant inference

questions.question: A production inference fleet hosts 100 distinct 7B-parameter models (26 GB memory footprint each) and 10 distinct 175B-parameter models (350 GB footprint each) on 80 GB A100 GPUs. According to the chapter's sharing economics analysis, which resource allocation strategy maximizes utilization while maintaining SLOs?
choices: Partition all GPUs uniformly into 1g.10gb MIG slices and shard the 175B models across 35 independent MIG slices.
Host all 100 small models on a single GPU using CPU offloading, and assign all remaining GPUs to the large models.
Co-locate the 7B models in pairs (2 models per GPU via MPS) to raise memory utilization from 33% to 65%, while reserving exclusive 8-GPU NVLink tensor-parallel groups for each 175B model.
Assign every 7B model its own dedicated 8-GPU cluster to guarantee sub-millisecond execution times.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Co-locate the 7B models in pairs (2 models per GPU via MPS) to raise memory utilization from 33% to 65%, while reserving exclusive 8-GPU NVLink tensor-parallel groups for each 175B model. A 7B model consumes 26 GB of an 80 GB A100, leaving 54 GB (67%) of expensive HBM unused under exclusive hosting (requiring 100 GPUs at 33% utilization). Packing 2 models per GPU via MPS consumes 52 GB, reducing the small-model requirement to 50 GPUs at 65% utilization and saving 50 GPUs ($876K/year). The large 175B models cannot be co-located because their 350 GB footprint demands 8 contiguous 80 GB GPUs communicating at high bandwidth over NVLink. Sharding 175B across MIG slices (Choice A) destroys NVLink tensor parallelism. CPU offloading (Choice B) causes severe latency collapse, and over-provisioning 8 GPUs per 7B model (Choice D) wastes massive capital.
questions.learning_objective: Design a bifurcated GPU sharing and exclusive-allocation strategy for heterogeneous inference fleets

questions.question: Traditional web load balancers route traffic using round-robin or least-outstanding-requests algorithms. Explain why these routing strategies cause tail latency spikes for Large Language Model serving, and describe what metric a memory-aware router must evaluate instead.
questions.answer: In standard web services, requests have relatively uniform computational cost. In LLM inference, request processing time and memory consumption vary by orders of magnitude based on prompt context length and generated output tokens. Least-outstanding-requests routing sends traffic to replicas based solely on active connection counts, ignoring the fact that a replica processing two 32K-context generation requests is heavily memory- and compute-saturated, while a replica processing five 100-token queries has ample headroom. A memory-aware LLM router tracks the real-time KV-cache occupancy and pending token counts of each replica: it routes long-context requests to replicas with sufficient contiguous KV-cache memory and short queries to higher-occupancy nodes, preventing cache thrashing, evictions, and out-of-memory stalls.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why memory-aware routing using KV-cache occupancy outperforms connection-based routing for LLMs

questions.question: Why does dynamic capacity sharing between training clusters and inference serving pools operate on diurnal 12- to 24-hour schedules rather than second-by-second traffic bursts?
choices: Data center power delivery systems require 6 hours of electrical stabilization before switching from training compute to inference compute.
Kubernetes and Slurm controllers can only synchronize state during midnight maintenance windows.
Network switches must be physically re-cabled whenever a GPU transitions between training and serving workloads.

Re-purposing a GPU node from training to serving requires 5 to 20 minutes of mode-switching latency (checkpointing training, terminating jobs, loading large model weights, and warming up compilation caches).
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Re-purposing a GPU node from training to serving requires 5 to 20 minutes of mode-switching latency (checkpointing training, terminating jobs, loading large model weights, and warming up compilation caches). Repurposing GPU hardware between batch training and interactive serving is not instantaneous: an active training job must execute a graceful checkpoint (1–5 min) and terminate, the node must join the serving pool, the serving engine must pull and load tens or hundreds of gigabytes of weights into GPU HBM (2–10 min), and warmup queries must populate kernel caches (1–5 min). This multi-minute overhead makes second-by-second capacity swapping impossible. Orchestrators instead shift large capacity blocks based on predictable diurnal demand curves (e.g., scaling up serving capacity at 7:30 AM ahead of morning traffic and returning nodes to training at 10:30 PM). Power systems, scheduler synchronization, and network fabrics do not impose multi-hour physical switching barriers.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the mode-switching overhead that bounds the timescale of dynamic training-serving capacity sharing

questions.question: Why do large multi-tenant GPU clusters implement hierarchical fair-share quotas with cross-team borrowing rather than rigid, static per-team GPU allocations?
choices: Rigid quotas force organizations to size every team for peak demand (stranding 25–40% of cluster capacity during off-peak periods), whereas borrowing lets idle capacity flow to teams with active demand while preserving guaranteed access via preemption.
Hierarchical quotas eliminate the need for GPU device drivers on worker nodes.
Static quotas are mathematically incapable of tracking clusters with more than two competing teams.
Cross-team borrowing permanently reassigns GPU hardware ownership to the team that submits the most jobs.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Rigid quotas force organizations to size every team for peak demand (stranding 25–40% of cluster capacity during off-peak periods), whereas borrowing lets idle capacity flow to teams with active demand while preserving guaranteed access via preemption. In practice, research and product teams have bursty, non-coincident demand peaks. Under static quotas, if Team A (500-GPU quota) is in a design lull using only 100 GPUs while Team B (300-GPU quota) has an urgent product deadline, 400 GPUs sit completely idle because Team B is forbidden from exceeding its quota. Hierarchical borrowing ($Q_{\text{effective}} = \min(Q_{\text{team}}, Q_{\text{dept}} - \sum U_{\text{allocated}})$) allows Team B to borrow Team A's idle GPUs as opportunistic, preemptible capacity, achieving high fleet utilization while guaranteeing that Team A can immediately reclaim its resources via preemption when needed. Drivers remain necessary, static quotas support arbitrary team counts, and borrowing is temporary rather than permanent.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate how hierarchical fair-share and borrowing balance team guarantees against aggregate fleet utilization

questions.question: Why must distributed training jobs executing on borrowed (opportunistic) quota maintain a significantly higher checkpoint frequency than jobs running on owned (guaranteed) quota?
questions.answer: Jobs running on borrowed capacity carry lower scheduling priority and are subject to immediate preemption whenever the owning team submits workloads requiring its guaranteed quota. If a borrowed job checkpoints infrequently (e.g., once every 4 hours) and is preempted 3.5 hours into a run, nearly 3.5 hours of expensive compute on hundreds of GPUs is completely lost. Maintaining an aggressive checkpoint cadence (or saving state immediately upon receiving preemption SIGTERM notices) minimizes the amount of lost progress per eviction event, ensuring that opportunistic computation remains economically productive despite frequent reclamation.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why opportunistic workloads must adapt checkpointing policies to preemption risk

questions.question: A cluster orchestrator configures a 1.4x over-subscription ratio on GPU compute resources. Under which workload conditions will this over-subscription policy succeed in improving cluster throughput without causing severe performance degradation?
choices: When all jobs run compute-saturated foundation model pretraining loops that maintain 99% continuous tensor core utilization.
When active jobs exhibit bursty, uncorrelated utilization profiles (e.g., alternating between CPU data preprocessing, disk I/O, and GPU kernel execution), averaging ~70% actual GPU utilization.
When jobs share GPU memory address spaces without container boundaries or process isolation.
When all workloads are single-threaded batch scripts running on host CPUs without GPU accelerators.
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. When active jobs exhibit bursty, uncorrelated utilization profiles (e.g., alternating between CPU data preprocessing, disk I/O, and GPU kernel execution), averaging ~70% actual GPU utilization. Over-subscription relies on statistical multiplexing: if jobs request 100% capacity but actually use only 70% due to data loading, evaluation phases, or host I/O, admitting $1.4\times$ as many jobs yields aggregate demand of $1.4 \times 0.70 = 0.98$ (98% physical capacity), maximizing utilization without contention. If workloads are compute-saturated pretraining runs at 99% utilization (Choice A), $1.4\times$ over-subscription causes immediate resource thrashing, memory contention, and performance collapse. Lack of process isolation (Choice C) causes security/stability failures, and CPU-only scripts (Choice D) do not utilize GPU over-subscription.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the statistical conditions required for safe cluster-wide resource over-subscription

questions.question: Explain why mature multi-tenant ML platforms enforce a strict 'no tag, no schedule' admission policy that rejects any job submission lacking team, project, or cost-center metadata.
questions.answer: Without mandatory team, project, and cost-center metadata attached at submission time, all GPU expenditures fall into an unassigned 'infrastructure' bucket. This creates a classic tragedy of the commons: individual engineering teams have no visibility into their financial burn, leading to quota hoarding, zombie jobs left running over weekends, and oversized GPU requests. Strict admission-time tagging provides the essential accounting substrate for Showback (reporting costs to teams) and Chargeback (billing departmental budgets). Transforming raw GPU consumption into attributable metrics ('Cost per Model Version', 'Cost per Experiment') forces teams to make economically rational trade-offs regarding model size, hyperparameter sweep breadth, and hardware efficiency.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why job attribution and metadata tagging are foundational to multi-tenant governance and FinOps

questions.question: In a heavily loaded multi-tenant cluster with multiple priority tiers, what is a preemption cascade, and how do schedulers prevent it?
choices: A physical failure where one GPU overheating triggers thermal emergency shutdowns in all adjacent server chassis.
A networking deadlock where AllReduce packets circle a fat-tree fabric indefinitely; prevented by spanning-tree protocols.
A database corruption in etcd caused by simultaneous pod termination requests; prevented by read-only replica scaling.

A chain reaction where evicting one job to free resources causes that job (or another displaced workload) to immediately preempt slightly lower-priority jobs across the cluster, thrashing the entire fleet; prevented by preemption cooldowns and holistic preemption.
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. A chain reaction where evicting one job to free resources causes that job (or another displaced workload) to immediately preempt slightly lower-priority jobs across the cluster, thrashing the entire fleet; prevented by preemption cooldowns and holistic preemption. A preemption cascade occurs when high-priority Job A preempts Priority-1 Job B. Job B is requeued and preempts Priority-2 Job C, which in turn preempts Priority-3 Job D. If checkpoint overheads are incurred at each step and evicted jobs immediately re-enter queues, the cluster spends massive compute cycles saving state, restarting, and thrashing rather than training. Schedulers prevent cascades by: (1) enforcing preemption cooldown periods, (2) providing holistic preemption that reserves auxiliary network/storage bandwidth for clean victim exits, and (3) restricting preemption paths to clear priority boundaries.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose preemption cascade failure modes and identify scheduling policies that mitigate them

questions.question: Why is multi-tenant GPU quota governance fundamentally an organizational and incentive-design challenge rather than merely an algorithmic scheduling problem?
questions.answer: Schedulers strictly enforce the mathematical rules they are configured with, but user behavior adapts strategically to policy incentives. When quotas are static and unyielding, teams hoard capacity, write persistent resubmission scripts, and submit dummy placeholder jobs to lock in GPU allocations before deadlines. If jobs are not billed to project budgets, researchers copy-paste maximum-GPU templates regardless of actual need. Technical algorithms (fair-share decay, preemption, capability matching) can only function effectively when paired with organizational incentives: clear priority hierarchies, departmental chargeback, quota expiration policies for unused allocations, and visibility into productive versus allocated utilization.
questions.learning_objective: Synthesize the organizational, behavioral, and technical dimensions of fleet quota governance
